name: Oats / rice-and-chicken carbs for bulking

card.summary: The cheap carb-and-chicken staple diet for a calorie-surplus bulk.
card.note: Larger surpluses add more body fat.

quick.overview:
This is the common bulking pattern of eating oats, rice and chicken in a calorie surplus to gain muscle.

The general principle of surplus eating for hypertrophy is widely accepted; the specific foods have not been trialled as a set.
quick.mechanism: A positive energy balance combined with adequate protein supports muscle growth alongside resistance training.
quick.risks: Larger surpluses and longer bulks add more body fat, and some lifters report needing a harder cut afterward.

lead: A "standard bulk" built on oats, rice and chicken means eating in a calorie surplus using inexpensive, easy-to-prepare carbohydrate and lean-protein staples so the body has the energy and amino acids to build muscle. The payoff people seek is a larger, fuller physique: more muscle on the frame, which also changes how shoulders, arms and chest look in clothes.

Wikipedia describes bulking as eating above maintenance needs and reports a well-established link between positive energy balance and muscle growth.[1] Oats are a calorie-dense grain (about 389 kcal and 17 g of protein per 100 g uncooked), and cooked white rice is a compact carbohydrate source (about 130 kcal and 29 g of carbohydrate per 100 g); chicken supplies protein.[2][3]

Bodybuilding references note that a larger surplus or a longer bulk adds more body fat, which is why lifters alternate bulking with a cutting phase.[1] No trial has tested oats, rice and chicken as a named bulking diet.

angle.text: These foods make it easy to hit a calorie and protein target at low cost, which supports gaining muscle alongside resistance training. The look people aim for is a bigger, more muscular build.

paras: Bodybuilders commonly alternate an off-season bulking phase with a pre-contest cut of roughly 12 to 14 weeks.[1] Clean bulking aims for muscle with limited fat gain, and dirty bulking uses a large surplus with less tracking; the latter tends to add more fat.[1]

Oats are usually eaten as oatmeal porridge or ground into flour, and contain about 4 g of soluble beta-glucan fibre per 100 g.[2] Rice is a staple food for over half of the world's population and is described as not a complete protein on its own, so pairing it with chicken or other protein foods is typical.[3]

Protein recommendations vary among experts, with some favouring about 1 g per pound of body weight and others more or less.[1] Controlled studies using calorimetry found no metabolic advantage of eating five to seven meals over three.[1]

A narrative review of food-first carbohydrate strategies for athletes lists oats and rice among mixed carbohydrate foods that are effective pre-exercise sources, while cautioning about gastrointestinal comfort and palatability when large quantities are needed.[4]

Randomised trials of oats against rice have been done in other contexts: a 2021 trial gave 210 mildly hypercholesterolaemic adults 80 g of oats or rice daily for 45 days and examined blood lipids and gut microbiota, and a 2025 trial compared low-gluten diets rich in oats or rice over 6 weeks in metabolically challenged volunteers.[5][6] These studies were not about muscle gain.

Forum posters describe eating large quantities of oats as part of weight-gain efforts, with one looksmax.org thread author saying they hoped it would have some positive effect.[7] Hacker News discussions in 2024 covered media stories on oats and weight management, which concern weight loss rather than bulking.[8][9]
No studies found on oats, rice and chicken as a specific bulking diet. Related trials compared oats with rice for cholesterol and gut-health outcomes.[5][6]

lore.intro: Cheap staples such as oats, rice and chicken are a recurring theme in lifting and looksmaxxing talk about gaining weight on a budget.

claims.claim: Oats and rice are an efficient way to reach a calorie surplus.
claims.believers: Posters describe forcing down large amounts of oats as a way to add mass, hoping for a positive effect on their physique.[7]
claims.experts: Oats and rice are calorie-providing grains, and energy surplus is linked to muscle growth in bodybuilding references.[1][2][3]

claims.claim: Oats mimic weight-loss drugs, so they are a poor choice for bulking.
claims.believers: Hacker News commenters discussed news stories that oats may aid weight management.[8]
claims.experts: Those stories concern satiety and weight loss in other populations; studies of oats against rice have examined cholesterol and gut bacteria.[5][6]
